prompt: Let $P(x)$ mean “$x$ is a program” and $T(x)$ mean “$x$ terminates”. Which formula negates “Every program terminates”, written $\forall x\,(P(x)\to T(x))$?

answers.explanation: To refute “every program terminates”, one program that does not terminate is enough. The quantifier changes from every to some, and the implication fails when P holds but T does not.
This is the original statement, not its negation.
One terminating program does not show that any program fails to terminate.
This says every object is a terminating program, rather than exhibiting a counterexample.
This says no program terminates. Negating “every program terminates” requires only one nonterminating program.
A nonterminating object that is not a program cannot refute a claim about programs.
A terminating object that is not a program is irrelevant to the claim.
This implication is true for any nonprogram, so such an object could satisfy the formula without refuting the original.
The witnesses may differ: a program could terminate while a different, nonprogram object does not. The counterexample must be the same object.
This concerns nonprograms; it does not assert that a program fails to terminate.
